Q5024.L1t: Lack of adequate sanitation is a major global public health problem, linked to diarrhoeal disease and child stunting.
Q5024.L2t: The WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme tracks open defecation worldwide, and the practice is concentrated in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.
Q5024.L3t: Global estimates for 2020 count several hundred million people with no toilet at all, out of a world population of about 7.8 billion, which works out to close to one person in ten.
Q5024.L4t: In 2020 roughly nine in a hundred people worldwide still practiced open defecation.
Q5024.L2f: Open defecation has been tracked globally only since 2015, and most of it occurs in high-income countries.
Q5024.L3f: By 2020 open defecation had been almost eliminated, with only a few tens of millions of people worldwide still lacking any toilet.
Q5024.L4f: In 2020 only a tiny sliver of the world population, about one in fifty people, still practiced open defecation.

Q5910.L1t: Land-use restrictions in residential subdivisions are commonly created by recorded declarations and enforced against later owners.
Q5910.L2t: Restriction (22) grants public utilities a right of way over the rear strip, while restriction (23) separately forbids building anywhere on that strip.
Q5910.L3t: Under a recorded general plan, a use restriction that binds later owners who have notice is enforced in equity by injunction at the suit of other lot owners, and the common-law categories of negative easement were limited to light, air, support and stream flow.
Q5910.L4t: The court will treat the ban on building as a restriction enforceable in equity against successors who took with notice of the recorded plan.
Q5910.L2f: Courts generally refuse to enforce any restriction in a recorded subdivision plan against a purchaser who did not personally sign the plan.
Q5910.L3f: A prohibition on building over a utility strip is treated by courts as a nonpossessory property interest that burdens the land at law, with no need for equitable enforcement.
Q5910.L4f: The court will construe the ban on building as an interest that prevents the servient owner from building, a right of the kind historically recognized as a negative easement.

Q5999.L1t: Public opinion on school desegregation was measured by national pollsters such as Gallup across the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s.
Q5999.L2t: Support for school desegregation rose over the decades in every region, and Southern respondents were consistently less supportive than those elsewhere.
Q5999.L3t: Even at the widest point, approval in the South was well above zero and approval in the rest of the country was well short of unanimous, so the regional gap was a difference of some tens of points rather than a near-total split.
Q5999.L4t: At its peak, approval outside the South exceeded approval in the South by about forty percentage points.
Q5999.L2f: Polls on school desegregation were first taken only after the 1970s, and they found little regional variation in views.
Q5999.L3f: At the peak of the divide, almost everyone outside the South approved of school desegregation while almost no one in the South did, leaving the South nearly the full scale below the rest of the country.
Q5999.L4f: At its peak, Southern approval was about eighty percentage points below approval in the rest of the country.
